Documentation is any written, recorded, or organized material that captures information — so that the information can be understood, used, referred back to, or proven later. Think of it as "putting things down in a form that lasts and communicates."

When something important happens, gets created, or needs to be explained, you can't just keep it only in someone's head. What if that person leaves? What if you forget? What if someone else needs to understand it? Documentation solves this. It is the act — and the result — of recording information in a clear, organized, and accessible way.

So "documentation" refers to:

  • The process of creating such records
  • The collection of records themselves

Both meanings are common, and context makes clear which one is meant.

Almost anything worth remembering or communicating:

  • A process or procedure — the steps to do something (e.g., how to operate a machine, how to file a tax return)
  • A decision — what was decided, by whom, and why
  • An agreement — what two or more parties promised each other (contracts, policies)
  • A product or system — how something works, how to use it, what its parts are
  • An event — what happened, when, and who was involved
  • An identity or status — proof of who you are or what qualifications you hold (e.g., a passport, a certificate, a medical record)

Documentation does not mean only paper. It includes:

  • Manuals and guides
  • Reports and summaries
  • Official certificates and licenses
  • Emails and letters (when kept as records)
  • Photographs, videos, audio recordings
  • Logs and registers (like a hospital patient's file)
  • Software comments and technical write-ups
  • Legal papers and contracts

What all of these share is intent: they are created deliberately to preserve and communicate information.

Documentation serves several important purposes:

  1. Memory — Humans forget. Organizations grow. Documentation ensures important information survives beyond individual memory.
  2. Clarity — When instructions or decisions are written down carefully, there is less room for misunderstanding or miscommunication.
  3. Proof — Documentation can serve as evidence. Your birth certificate documents your birth. A signed receipt documents a transaction. In disputes, documentation is often the deciding factor.
  4. Consistency — When a process is documented, every person who follows it can do so the same way. This is critical in medicine, law, engineering, and many other fields.
  5. Learning and onboarding — When someone new joins a team or studies a subject, documentation helps them get up to speed without needing someone to explain everything from scratch.
  6. Accountability — Records of who did what, when, and why create accountability, which is important in workplaces, governments, and legal systems.

The word is used across many fields, and while the core meaning stays the same, the flavor changes slightly:

  • In software and technology, documentation refers to written explanations of how a program or system works — for users ("user documentation") or for developers ("technical documentation"). Good software documentation makes the difference between a tool people can use and one that frustrates them.
  • In medicine, documentation means patient records — symptoms, diagnoses, treatments, test results. Accurate medical documentation is a legal and ethical obligation.
  • In law and business, documentation refers to the formal papers and records that support a claim, a transaction, a contract, or a project. "Do you have documentation for that?" means "Can you prove it with written records?"
  • In immigration, documentation refers to official papers that prove your identity, nationality, or legal status (passport, visa, work permit).
  • In research and academia, documentation means citing your sources and keeping records of your data and methods — so others can verify or build upon your work.

A document is a single item — one paper, one file, one record.

Documentation (usually uncountable, or treated as a collective noun) refers to the whole body of such material. For example, "the documentation for this software" means all the manuals, guides, and reference materials together — not just one page.

However, "documentations" (plural) is occasionally used when referring to several distinct sets of records or bodies of documentation — though this is less common.
A simple way to remember it

If you ever wonder what documentation means, ask yourself: "Has this been written down properly so someone else can understand, use, verify, or learn from it?" If the answer is yes, what you're holding — or what was created — is documentation.
